metadata.title: Compressing Neural Language Models by Sparse Word Representations

extraction_notes.note: Table 1 (parameter counts per subnet) and the perplexity/memory tables are floats, not text; their content is cited by the claims ClP1, ClP6-ClP11 rather than extracted as nodes.
The 'tricks' paragraph is a modification of the sparse-coding solver; extracted as an unmarked algorithm with three steps, the reformulated objective inside it as a problem.
theorem or claim: a cited NCE self-normalization result stated loosely in one sentence; typed theorem/external because it is a cited prior result.

ss:eval.LM.section: Quantitative Analysis of Compressed Language Models

nodes.name: n-gram language model
nodes.statement: Traditional $n$-gram models impose a Markov assumption that a word is only dependent on previous $n-1$ words and independent of its position.
differentia: a word is only dependent on previous $n-1$ words and independent of its position

nodes.name: Embedding/Encoding/Prediction decomposition of a neural LM
nodes.statement: In the above models, we can view that a neural LM is composed of three main parts, namely the \texttt{Embedding}{}, \texttt{Encoding}{}, and \texttt{Prediction}{} subnets, as shown in Figure~\ref{fig:sNLM}.
nodes.statement_short: A neural LM consists of three subnets: Embedding, Encoding and Prediction.

nodes.name: Embedding subnet
nodes.statement: The \texttt{Embedding}{} subnet maps a word to a dense vector, representing some abstract features of the word \cite{word2vec}. Note that this subnet usually accepts a list of words (known as history or context words) and outputs a sequence of word embeddings.

nodes.name: Encoding subnet
nodes.statement: The \texttt{Encoding}{} subnet encodes the history of a target word into a dense vector (known as \textit{context} or \textit{history} representation). We may either leverage FFNNs \cite{NLM} or RNNs \cite{RNNLM} as the \texttt{Encoding}{} subnet, but RNNs typically yield a better performance \cite{Sundermeyer:2015gj}.

nodes.name: Prediction subnet (softmax output layer)
nodes.statement: The \texttt{Prediction}{} subnet outputs a distribution of target words as \begin{align} p(w = w_i|h) = &\dfrac{\exp(s(h, w_i))} {\sum_j \exp(s(h, w_j))}, \\ s(h, w_i) = & \trans{\vector{W}_i} \vector{h} + b_i, \end{align} where $\vector{h}$ is the vector representation of context/history $h$, obtained by the \texttt{Encoding}{} subnet. $\vector{W} = (\vector{W}_1, \vector{W}_2, \dots, \vector{W}_V) \in \mathbb{R}^{C\times V}$ is the \textit{output weights} of \texttt{Prediction}; $\vector{b} = (b_1, b_2, \dots, b_V) \in \mathbb{R}^{C}$ is the bias (the prior). $s(h, w_i)$ is a scoring function indicating the degree to which the context $h$ matches a target word $w_i$. ($V$ is the size of vocabulary $\mathcal{V}$; $C$ is the dimension of context/history, given by the \texttt{Encoding}{} subnet.)
nodes.statement_short: Softmax over scores $s(h,w_i)=W_i^\top h + b_i$ with output weights $W\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times V}$ and biases $b$.

nodes.name: Softmax output distribution and scoring function
nodes.statement: p(w = w_i|h) = &\dfrac{\exp(s(h, w_i))} {\sum_j \exp(s(h, w_j))}, \\ s(h, w_i) = & \trans{\vector{W}_i} \vector{h} + b_i,
nodes.label: eq:sNNLM

nodes.name: Normalization factor dominates time complexity
nodes.statement: Training neural LMs is typically time-consuming especially when the vocabulary size is large. The normalization factor in Equation~(\ref{eq:sNNLM}) contributes most to time complexity.

nodes.name: Embedding and Prediction parameters grow linearly in vocabulary size
nodes.statement: The number of parameters in the \texttt{Embedding}{} and \texttt{Prediction}{} subnets in neural LMs increases linearly with respect to the vocabulary size, which is large (Table~\ref{tab:no.param}).
conclusions: The number of parameters in the \texttt{Embedding}{} and \texttt{Prediction}{} subnets in neural LMs increases linearly with respect to the vocabulary size

nodes.name: Base set of common words
nodes.statement: We split the vocabulary $\mathcal{V}$ into two disjoint subsets ($\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$). The first subset $\mathcal{B}$ is a base set, containing a fixed number of common words (8k in our experiments).
differentia: containing a fixed number of common words

nodes.name: Set of uncommon words
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{V}\backslash \mathcal{B}$ is a set of uncommon words.

nodes.name: Sparse code
nodes.statement: Following most work in the literature \cite{sparse,sparse2}, we represent each uncommon word with a sparse, linear combination of common ones' embeddings. The sparse coefficients are called a \textit{sparse code} for a given word.
differentia: each uncommon word with a sparse, linear combination of common ones' embeddings

nodes.name: Embedding matrix of common words
nodes.statement: Suppose $\vector{U}=(\vector{U}_1, \vector{U}_2, \dots, \vector{U}_B) \in \mathbb{R}^{E\times B}$ is the (learned) embedding matrix of common words, i.e., $\vector{U}_i$ is the embedding of $i$-th word in $\mathcal{B}$. (Here, $B=|\mathcal{B}|$.)

nodes.name: Natural (one-hot) sparse code of a base word
nodes.statement: Each word in $\mathcal{B}$ has a natural sparse code (denoted as $\vector{x}$): it is a one-hot vector with $B$ elements, the $i$-th dimension being on for the $i$-th word in $\mathcal{B}$.

nodes.name: Sparse code of an uncommon word
nodes.statement: For a word $w\in \mathcal{C}$, we shall learn a sparse vector $\vector{x} = (x_1, x_2, \dots, x_B)$ as the sparse code of the word.

nodes.name: Embedding of an uncommon word from its sparse code
nodes.statement: \hat{\vector{w}} = \sum_{j=1}^B x_j \vector{U}_j = \vector{U}\vector{x},
nodes.statement_short: The embedding of a rare word is $\hat w = Ux$.
nodes.label: eq:sp2dense

nodes.name: Sparse coding objective for rare words
nodes.statement: To learn the sparse representation of a certain word $w$, we propose the following optimization objective \begin{align} \min_{\vector x}\ \ & \| \vector{Ux} - \vector{w} \|_{2}^{2} + \alpha \|\vector{x}\|_1 + \beta |\trans{\vector{1}} \vector{x} - 1| \nonumber\\ &{} + \gamma \trans{\vector{1}} \max \{\vector{0}, -\vector{x}\}, \end{align} where $\max$ denotes the component-wise maximum; $\vector{w}$ is the embedding for a rare word $w\in \mathcal{C}$.
nodes.statement_short: Fit $Ux\approx w$ with $\ell_1$ sparsity, sum-to-one and nonnegativity penalties.

nodes.name: Sparse coding objective
nodes.statement: \min_{\vector x}\ \ & \| \vector{Ux} - \vector{w} \|_{2}^{2} + \alpha \|\vector{x}\|_1 + \beta |\trans{\vector{1}} \vector{x} - 1| \nonumber\\ &{} + \gamma \trans{\vector{1}} \max \{\vector{0}, -\vector{x}\},
nodes.label: eq:opt_sp

nodes.name: Fitting loss
nodes.statement: The first term (called \textit{fitting loss} afterwards) evaluates the closeness between a word's coded vector representation and its ``true'' representation $\vector{w}$, which is the general goal of sparse coding.

nodes.name: Role of the regularization terms
nodes.statement: The second term is an $\ell_1$ regularizer, which encourages a sparse solution. The last two regularization terms favor a solution that sums to 1 and that is nonnegative, respectively. The nonnegative regularizer is applied as in \newcite{document} due to psychological interpretation concerns.

nodes.name: Sparse code learning with adaptive regularization weights
nodes.statement: It is difficult to determine the hyperparameters $\alpha$, $\beta$, and $\gamma$. Therefore we perform several tricks. First, we drop the last term in the problem \eqref{eq:opt_sp}, but clip each element in $\vector{x}$ so that all the sparse codes are nonnegative during each update of training. Second, we re-parametrize $\alpha$ and $\beta$ by balancing the fitting loss and regularization terms dynamically during training. Concretely, we solve the following optimization problem, which is slightly different but closely related to the conceptual objective \eqref{eq:opt_sp}: \begin{equation} \min_{\vector{x}}\ \ L(\vector{x}) + \alpha_t R_1(\vector{x}) + \beta_t R_2(\vector{x}), \end{equation} where $L(\vector{x}) = \| \vector{Ux} - \vector{w} \|_{2}^{2}$, $R_1(\vector{x}) = \|\vector{x}\|_1$, and $R_2(\vector{x}) = |\trans{\vector{1}} \vector{x} - 1|$. $\alpha_t$ and $\beta_t$ are adaptive parameters that are resolved during training time. Suppose $\vector{x}_t$ is the value we obtain after the update of the $t$-th step, we expect the importance of fitness and regularization remain unchanged during training. This is equivalent to \begin{align} \dfrac{\alpha_t R_1(\vector{x}_t)}{L(\vector{x}_t)} = w_\alpha &\equiv \mbox{const}, \\ \dfrac{\beta_t R_2(\vector{x}_t)}{L(\vector{x}_t)} = w_\beta &\equiv \mbox{const}. \end{align} or \[ \alpha_t = \dfrac{L(\vector{x}_t)}{R_1(\vector{x}_t)} w_\alpha \text{ and } \beta_t = \dfrac{L(\vector{x}_t)}{R_2(\vector{x}_t)} w_\beta, \] where $w_\alpha$ and $w_\beta$ are the ratios between the regularization loss and the fitting loss. They are much easier to specify than $\alpha$ or $\beta$ in the problem~\eqref{eq:opt_sp}.
nodes.statement_short: Solve the sparse-coding objective by dropping the nonnegativity term in favour of clipping and rescaling $\alpha_t,\beta_t$ each step to keep fixed ratios $w_\alpha,w_\beta$ of regularization to fitting loss.

nodes.name: Drop nonnegativity term, clip codes
nodes.statement: First, we drop the last term in the problem \eqref{eq:opt_sp}, but clip each element in $\vector{x}$ so that all the sparse codes are nonnegative during each update of training.
nodes.statement_short: Replace the nonnegativity penalty by clipping $x$ to be nonnegative at each update.

nodes.name: Solve the re-parametrized objective
nodes.statement: Second, we re-parametrize $\alpha$ and $\beta$ by balancing the fitting loss and regularization terms dynamically during training. Concretely, we solve the following optimization problem, which is slightly different but closely related to the conceptual objective \eqref{eq:opt_sp}: \begin{equation} \min_{\vector{x}}\ \ L(\vector{x}) + \alpha_t R_1(\vector{x}) + \beta_t R_2(\vector{x}), \end{equation} where $L(\vector{x}) = \| \vector{Ux} - \vector{w} \|_{2}^{2}$, $R_1(\vector{x}) = \|\vector{x}\|_1$, and $R_2(\vector{x}) = |\trans{\vector{1}} \vector{x} - 1|$. $\alpha_t$ and $\beta_t$ are adaptive parameters that are resolved during training time.
nodes.statement_short: Minimize $L+\alpha_t R_1+\beta_t R_2$ with adaptive weights.

nodes.name: Sparse coding objective with adaptive weights
nodes.statement: Concretely, we solve the following optimization problem, which is slightly different but closely related to the conceptual objective \eqref{eq:opt_sp}: \begin{equation} \min_{\vector{x}}\ \ L(\vector{x}) + \alpha_t R_1(\vector{x}) + \beta_t R_2(\vector{x}), \end{equation} where $L(\vector{x}) = \| \vector{Ux} - \vector{w} \|_{2}^{2}$, $R_1(\vector{x}) = \|\vector{x}\|_1$, and $R_2(\vector{x}) = |\trans{\vector{1}} \vector{x} - 1|$. $\alpha_t$ and $\beta_t$ are adaptive parameters that are resolved during training time.
nodes.statement_short: Minimize fitting loss plus adaptively weighted $\ell_1$ and sum-to-one penalties.

nodes.name: Adaptive sparse coding objective
nodes.statement: \min_{\vector{x}}\ \ L(\vector{x}) + \alpha_t R_1(\vector{x}) + \beta_t R_2(\vector{x}),
nodes.label: eq:opt_sp_trick

nodes.name: Set adaptive weights by fixed loss ratios
nodes.statement: Suppose $\vector{x}_t$ is the value we obtain after the update of the $t$-th step, we expect the importance of fitness and regularization remain unchanged during training. This is equivalent to \begin{align} \dfrac{\alpha_t R_1(\vector{x}_t)}{L(\vector{x}_t)} = w_\alpha &\equiv \mbox{const}, \\ \dfrac{\beta_t R_2(\vector{x}_t)}{L(\vector{x}_t)} = w_\beta &\equiv \mbox{const}. \end{align} or \[ \alpha_t = \dfrac{L(\vector{x}_t)}{R_1(\vector{x}_t)} w_\alpha \text{ and } \beta_t = \dfrac{L(\vector{x}_t)}{R_2(\vector{x}_t)} w_\beta, \] where $w_\alpha$ and $w_\beta$ are the ratios between the regularization loss and the fitting loss. They are much easier to specify than $\alpha$ or $\beta$ in the problem~\eqref{eq:opt_sp}.
nodes.statement_short: Set $\alpha_t=w_\alpha L(x_t)/R_1(x_t)$, $\beta_t=w_\beta L(x_t)/R_2(x_t)$.

nodes.name: Constant regularization-to-fitting ratios
nodes.statement: \dfrac{\alpha_t R_1(\vector{x}_t)}{L(\vector{x}_t)} = w_\alpha &\equiv \mbox{const}, \\ \dfrac{\beta_t R_2(\vector{x}_t)}{L(\vector{x}_t)} = w_\beta &\equiv \mbox{const}.
nodes.label: eq:alpha

nodes.name: True embeddings from word2vec
nodes.statement: To learn the sparse codes, we first train the ``true'' embeddings by {\tt word2vec}\footnote{https://code.google.com/archive/p/word2vec} for both common words and rare words. However, these true embeddings are slacked during our language modeling.

nodes.name: Sparse codes are fixed, non-tunable and tiny
nodes.statement: As the codes are pre-computed and remain unchanged during language modeling, they are not tunable parameters of our neural model. Considering the learned sparse codes, we need only 4--8 values for each word on average, as the codes contain 0.05--0.1\% non-zero values, which are almost negligible.

nodes.name: Compressed Embedding subnet
nodes.statement: We leverage the sparse representation of words mentioned above to construct a compressed \texttt{Embedding}{} subnet, where the number of parameters is independent of the vocabulary size. By solving the optimization problem \eqref{eq:opt_sp_trick} for each word, we obtain a non-negative sparse code $\vector{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{B}$ for each word, indicating the degree to which the word is related to common words in $\mathcal{B}$. Then the embedding of a word is given by $\hat{\vector{w}}=\vector{U}\vector{x}$.
nodes.statement_short: Each word's embedding is $Ux$ with its fixed nonnegative sparse code $x$, so the parameters do not depend on the vocabulary.

nodes.name: Compressed embeddings are dense
nodes.statement: We would like to point out that the embedding of a word $\hat{\vector{w}}$ is not sparse because $\vector{U}$ is a dense matrix, which serves as a shared parameter of learning all words' vector representations.

nodes.name: Base output weights and biases
nodes.statement: Without loss of generality, we let $\vector{D} = \vector{W}_{:,1:B}$ be the output weights of $B$ base target words, and $\vector{c} = \vector{b}_{1:B}$ be bias of the $B$ target words.\footnote{ $\vector{W}_{:,1:B}$ is the first $B$ columns of $\vector{W}$.}

nodes.name: Sharing sparse codes between embeddings and output weights
nodes.statement: We claim that it is reasonable to share the same set of sparse codes to represent word vectors in \texttt{Embedding}{} and the output weights in the \texttt{Prediction}{} subnet.
conclusions: it is reasonable to share the same set of sparse codes to represent word vectors in \texttt{Embedding}{} and the output weights in the \texttt{Prediction}{} subnet

nodes.name: Argument for sharing sparse codes
nodes.statement: In a given corpus, an occurrence of a word is always companied by its context. The co-occurrence statistics about a word or corresponding context are the same. As both word embedding and context vectors capture these co-occurrence statistics \cite{Levy:2014wb}, we can expect that context vectors share the same internal structure as embeddings. Moreover, for a fine-trained network, given any word $w$ and its context $h$, the output layer's weight vector corresponding to $w$ should specify a large inner-product score for the context $h$; thus these context vectors should approximate the weight vector of $w$. Therefore, word embeddings and the output weight vectors should share the same internal structures and it is plausible to use a same set of sparse representations for both words and target-word weight vectors.
nodes.statement_short: Heuristic argument: embeddings and context vectors capture the same co-occurrence statistics, and context vectors approximate the output weight vector, so both share structure.

nodes.name: Co-occurrence argument
nodes.statement: In a given corpus, an occurrence of a word is always companied by its context. The co-occurrence statistics about a word or corresponding context are the same. As both word embedding and context vectors capture these co-occurrence statistics \cite{Levy:2014wb}, we can expect that context vectors share the same internal structure as embeddings.
nodes.statement_short: Embeddings and context vectors capture the same co-occurrence statistics.

nodes.name: Context vectors approximate output weights
nodes.statement: Moreover, for a fine-trained network, given any word $w$ and its context $h$, the output layer's weight vector corresponding to $w$ should specify a large inner-product score for the context $h$; thus these context vectors should approximate the weight vector of $w$.
nodes.statement_short: Large inner-product scores make context vectors approximate the target weight vector.

nodes.name: Conclude shared structure
nodes.statement: Therefore, word embeddings and the output weight vectors should share the same internal structures and it is plausible to use a same set of sparse representations for both words and target-word weight vectors.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude one set of sparse codes can serve both.

nodes.name: Compressed Prediction subnet
nodes.statement: Formally, the $i$-th output weight vector is estimated by \begin{equation} \hat{\vector{W}}_i = \vector{D} \vector{x}_i, \end{equation} The biases can also be compressed as \begin{equation} \hat{b}_i = \vector{c} \vector{x}_i. \end{equation} where $\vector{x}_i$ is the sparse representation of the $i$-th word. (It is shared in the compression of weights and biases.)
nodes.statement_short: Output weights and biases of every word are $Dx_i$ and $cx_i$ using the same sparse code $x_i$.

nodes.name: Compressed output weight vector
nodes.statement: \hat{\vector{W}}_i = \vector{D} \vector{x}_i,
nodes.label: eq:sp2detector

nodes.name: Compressed output bias
nodes.statement: \hat{b}_i = \vector{c} \vector{x}_i.
nodes.label: eq:sp2detector_bias

nodes.name: Parameter count independent of vocabulary
nodes.statement: In the above model, we have managed to compressed a language model whose number of parameters is irrelevant to the vocabulary size.
conclusions: a language model whose number of parameters is irrelevant to the vocabulary size

nodes.name: Uncompressed-bias variant
nodes.statement: To better estimate a ``prior'' distribution of words, we may alternatively assign an independent bias to each word, i.e., $\vector{b}$ is not compressed.

nodes.name: Independent biases add negligible parameters
nodes.statement: In this variant, the number of model parameters grows very slowly and is also negligible because each word needs only one extra parameter.
conclusions: the number of model parameters grows very slowly and is also negligible

nodes.name: Noise-contrastive estimation (NCE)
nodes.statement: NCE generates a few negative samples for each positive data sample. During training, we only need to compute the unnormalized probability of these positive and negative samples.

nodes.name: Normalized model probability with context-dependent normalization factor
nodes.statement: Formally, the estimated probability of the word $w_i$ with history/context $h$ is \begin{align} P(w|h; \vector{\theta}) &= \dfrac{1}{Z_h} P^0(w_i|h; \vector{\theta})\nonumber \\ &= \dfrac1{Z_h}\exp(s(w_i,h;\vector{\theta})), \end{align} where $\bm\theta$ is the parameters and $Z_h$ is a context-dependent normalization factor. $P^0(w_i|h; \vector{\theta})$ is the unnormalized probability of the $w$ (given by the SpUnnrmProb layer in Figure~\ref{fig:NCE-regression}).
nodes.statement_short: $P(w|h;\theta)=Z_h^{-1}\exp(s(w,h;\theta))$ with context-dependent normalizer $Z_h$.

nodes.name: Normalized language model probability
nodes.statement: P(w|h; \vector{\theta}) &= \dfrac{1}{Z_h} P^0(w_i|h; \vector{\theta})\nonumber \\ &= \dfrac1{Z_h}\exp(s(w_i,h;\vector{\theta})),
nodes.label: eq:nrm_lang_model

nodes.name: Unit normalization factor in base model
nodes.statement: Following \newcite{Mnih:2012tv}, we set $Z_h=1$ for all $h$ in the base model (without \texttt{ZRegression}).

nodes.name: NCE objective per context
nodes.statement: The objective for each occurrence of context/history $h$ is \begin{align*} J(\vector{\theta}|h) = & \log \dfrac{P(w_i|h;\vector{\theta})} {P(w_i|h;\vector{\theta}) + k P_n(w_i)} + \\ & \sum_{j=1}^{k} \log \dfrac{kP_n(w_j)} {P(w_j|h;\vector{\theta}) + k P_n(w_j)}, \end{align*} where $P_n(w)$ is the probability of drawing a negative sample $w$; $k$ is the number of negative samples that we draw for each positive sample.
nodes.statement_short: Per-context NCE log-likelihood of classifying the true word against $k$ noise samples.

nodes.name: Overall NCE objective
nodes.statement: The overall objective of NCE is \begin{equation*} J(\vector{\theta}) = \mathbb{E}_h [J(\vector{\theta}|h)] \approx \dfrac{1}{M} \sum_{i=1}^{M} J(\vector{\theta}|h_i), \end{equation*} where $h_i$ is an occurrence of the context and $M$ is the total number of context occurrences.
nodes.statement_short: Expected per-context objective, approximated by the empirical average over context occurrences.

nodes.name: Instability when the normalization factor is far from 1
nodes.statement: Although setting $Z_h$ to 1 generally works well in our experiment, we find that in certain scenarios, the model is unstable. Experiments show that when the true normalization factor is far away from 1, the cost function may vibrate.

nodes.name: ZRegression
nodes.statement: To comply with NCE in general, we therefore propose a \texttt{ZRegression} layer to predict the normalization constant $Z_h$ dependent on $h$, instead of treating it as a constant. The regression layer is computed by \[ Z_h^{-1} = \exp(\trans{\vector{W}_Z}\vector{h}+b_Z), \] where $\vector{W}_Z\in \mathbb{R}^{C}$ and $b_Z\in \mathbb{R}$ are weights and bias for \texttt{ZRegression}. Hence, the estimated probability by NCE with \texttt{ZRegression} is given by \begin{equation*}\nonumber P(w|h) = \exp(s(h,w)) \cdot \exp(\trans{\vector{W}_Z}\vector{h}+b_Z). \end{equation*}
differentia: to predict the normalization constant $Z_h$ dependent on $h$
nodes.statement_short: A regression layer predicting $Z_h^{-1}=\exp(W_Z^\top h+b_Z)$ from the context vector, multiplied into the unnormalized probability.

nodes.name: ZRegression does not guarantee normalization
nodes.statement: Note that the \texttt{ZRegression} layer does not guarantee normalized probabilities. During validation and testing, we explicitly normalize the probabilities by Equation~\eqref{eq:sNNLM}.

nodes.name: Learned sparse codes are meaningful
nodes.statement: The qualitative analysis demonstrates that our approach can indeed learn a sparse code of a word, and that the codes are meaningful.
conclusions: our approach can indeed learn a sparse code of a word, and that the codes are meaningful

nodes.name: Perplexity
nodes.statement: We take perplexity as the performance measurement of a language model, which is defined by \[ \mathrm{PPL} = 2^{-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\log_2 p(w_i|h_i)} \] where $N$ is the number of running words in the test corpus.
nodes.section: 4.3 Quantitative Analysis of Compressed Language Models
nodes.statement_short: $\mathrm{PPL}=2^{-\frac1N\sum\log_2 p(w_i|h_i)}$ over the test corpus.

nodes.name: KN3
nodes.statement: \textbf{KN3}. We adopted the modified Kneser-Ney smoothing technique to train a 3-gram LM; we used the SRILM toolkit \cite{toolkit} in out experiment.

nodes.name: LBL5
nodes.statement: \textbf{LBL5}. A \textbf{L}og-\textbf{B}i\textbf{L}inear model introduced in \newcite{three}. We used 5 preceding words as context.

nodes.name: LSTM-s
nodes.statement: \textbf{LSTM-s}. A standard LSTM-RNN language model which is applied in \newcite{Sundermeyer:2015gj} and \newcite{visualize}. We implemented the LM ourselves based on Theano \cite{2016arXiv160502688short} and also used NCE for training.

nodes.name: LSTM-z
nodes.statement: \textbf{LSTM-z}. An LSTM-RNN enhanced with the \texttt{ZRegression} mechanism described in Section~\ref{ss:NCE}.

nodes.name: LSTM-z,wb
nodes.statement: \textbf{LSTM-z$,$wb}. Based on LSTM-z, we compressed word embeddings in \texttt{Embedding}{} and the output weights and biases in \texttt{Prediction}{}.

nodes.name: LSTM-z,w
nodes.statement: \textbf{LSTM-z$,$w}. In this variant, we did not compress the bias term in the output layer. For each word in $\mathcal{C}$, we assigned an independent bias parameter.

nodes.name: LSTM LMs outperform LBL and KN3
nodes.statement: As we see, LSTM-based LMs significantly outperform the log-bilinear model as well as the backoff 3-gram LM, even if the 3-gram LM is trained on a much larger corpus with 1.6 billion words.
conclusions: LSTM-based LMs significantly outperform the log-bilinear model as well as the backoff 3-gram LM

nodes.name: ZRegression improves LSTM perplexity
nodes.statement: The {\tt ZRegression} mechanism improves the performance of LSTM to a large extent, which is unexpected.
conclusions: The {\tt ZRegression} mechanism improves the performance of LSTM to a large extent

nodes.name: Compressed LMs match or beat LSTM-z
nodes.statement: Regarding the compression method proposed in this paper, we notice that LSTM-z$,$wb and LSTM\nobreakdash-z$,$w yield similar performance to LSTM-z. In particular, LSTM-z$,$w outperforms LSTM-z in all scenarios of different vocabulary sizes.
conclusions: LSTM-z$,$wb and LSTM\nobreakdash-z$,$w yield similar performance to LSTM-z
LSTM-z$,$w outperforms LSTM-z in all scenarios of different vocabulary sizes

nodes.name: Up to 80% memory reduction
nodes.statement: Moreover, both LSTM-z$,$wb and LSTM-z$,$w can reduce the memory consumption by up to $80\%$ (Table~\ref{tab:para}).
conclusions: both LSTM-z$,$wb and LSTM-z$,$w can reduce the memory consumption by up to $80\%$

nodes.name: Performance trend versus vocabulary size
nodes.statement: We see such a tendency that compressed LMs (LSTM-z$,$wb and LSTM-z$,$w, yellow and red lines) are generally better than LSTM-z (black line) when we have a small vocabulary. However, LSTM-z$,$wb is slightly worse than LSTM-z if the vocabulary size is greater than, say, 20k. The LSTM-z$,$w remains comparable to LSTM-z as the vocabulary grows.
conclusions: compressed LMs (LSTM-z$,$wb and LSTM-z$,$w, yellow and red lines) are generally better than LSTM-z (black line) when we have a small vocabulary

nodes.name: Information loss versus better rare-word estimation
nodes.statement: To explain this phenomenon, we may imagine that the compression using sparse codes has two effects: it loses information, but it also enables more accurate estimation of parameters especially for rare words. When the second factor dominates, we can reasonably expect a high performance of the compressed LM.

nodes.name: Compressed parameter count barely grows with vocabulary
nodes.statement: From the bars in Figure~\ref{fig:performance}, we observe that traditional LMs have a parameter space growing linearly with the vocabulary size. But the number of parameters in our compressed models does not increase---or strictly speaking, increases at an extremely small rate---with vocabulary.
conclusions: the number of parameters in our compressed models does not increase---or strictly speaking, increases at an extremely small rate---with vocabulary

nodes.name: NCE training without ZRegression becomes unstable
nodes.statement: As shown in Figure~\ref{fig:zregression}a, the training process becomes unstable after processing 70\% of the dataset: the training loss vibrates significantly, whereas the test loss increases.
conclusions: the training process becomes unstable after processing 70\% of the dataset

nodes.name: Instability correlates with the normalization factor
nodes.statement: We find a strong correlation between unstableness and the $Z_h$ factor in Equation~\eqref{eq:nrm_lang_model}, i.e., the sum of unnormalized probability (Figure~\ref{fig:zregression}b).
conclusions: a strong correlation between unstableness and the $Z_h$ factor

nodes.name: Self-normalization of NCE

nodes.name: ZRegression estimates Z_h and stabilizes training
nodes.statement: We propose the \texttt{ZRegression} mechanism in Section~\ref{ss:NCE}, which can estimate the $Z_h$ factor well (Figure~\ref{fig:zregression}d) based on the history vector $\vector{h}$. In this way, we manage to stabilize the training process (Figure~\ref{fig:zregression}c) and improve the performance by a large margin, as has shown in Table~\ref{tab:ppl}.

nodes.name: ZRegression applies to any NCE-trained LM
nodes.statement: It should be mentioned that \texttt{ZRegression} is not specific to model compression and is generally applicable to other neural LMs trained by NCE.
